Two conservation laws are needed together: **momentum** fixes the ratio of the speeds,
**energy** fixes their size.
**Step 1 — conserve momentum.** Gun and shell start at rest, so
(0·2)v = (4)V
**V = v/20 = 0·05v**
where v is the shell's speed and V the gun's recoil speed, in opposite directions.
**Step 2 — write the energy released.** The explosion's 1·05 kJ becomes the kinetic
energy of both:
½(0·2)v² + ½(4)V² = 1050
**Step 3 — substitute V = 0·05v.**
0·1v² + 2(0·0025v²) = 1050
0·1v² + 0·005v² = 1050
**0·105 v² = 1050**
**Step 4 — solve.**
v² = 10000
**v = 100 m s⁻¹** ✓
and the gun recoils at V = **5 m s⁻¹**.
**Why both laws are needed.** Momentum alone gives only the **ratio** 20 : 1 of the
speeds; energy alone cannot separate the two unknowns ✓ Together they pin both down.
**Where the energy goes.**
shell: ½(0·2)(100²) = **1000 J**
gun: ½(4)(5²) = **50 J**
total = **1050 J** ✓ exactly the energy released, confirming the answer.
**Why the light shell takes almost all the energy.** The two carry **equal momentum** p,
and kinetic energy is p²/2m ✓ so energy is shared **inversely** as the mass: the 0·2 kg
shell gets twenty times the energy of the 4 kg gun. That is the whole point of a light
projectile and a heavy gun - and why the recoil is survivable.
**Reading the distractors.** **80, 40 and 120 m s⁻¹** ✗ would give total energies of 672,
168 and 1512 J - none of them 1050 ✓ Substituting back into the energy equation is the
quickest way to test any candidate.
**A shortcut.** Because the gun takes only 1/21 of the energy, the shell's energy is
1050 x 20/21 = **1000 J**, so ½(0·2)v² = 1000 and v = 100 m s⁻¹ ✓
∴ 100 m/s.

The insect climbs until the slope outruns the friction available, and that threshold is
set by tan α = μ.
**Step 1 — identify the slope angle.** With α measured from the **vertical** at the
centre of the hemisphere, the surface at the insect's position is inclined at **α** to
the horizontal ✓ So the insect is effectively on a plane of angle α.
**Step 2 — resolve the weight.**
normal to the surface: **mg cos α**, so N = mg cos α
along the surface: **mg sin α**, pulling it back down
**Step 3 — impose the limiting-friction condition.** The greatest friction available is
μN, so the highest point the insect can reach satisfies
mg sin α = μ mg cos α
**tan α = μ = 1/3**
**Step 4 — express it as the options do.**
cot α = 1/tan α = **3** ✓
**Why this is the "maximum possible α".** Below it, mg sin α is less than μ mg cos α and
friction holds the insect comfortably. Above it the demand exceeds the supply and the
insect slides ✓ So cot α = 3 marks the exact boundary.
**Why "very slowly" matters.** Crawling slowly means no acceleration, so the forces
simply balance ✓ A sudden movement would need extra friction and the insect would slip
lower down.
**The numerical angle.** tan α = 0·333 gives α = **18·4°** from the vertical - the insect
manages only a short way up the bowl, because μ = 1/3 is quite slippery ✓
**The height it reaches.** With cot α = 3, cos α = 3/√10 = 0·949, so for a bowl of radius
R the insect rises R(1 − cos α) = **0·051R** - about a twentieth of the radius ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **sec α = 3** ✗ gives cos α = 1/3 and tan α = 2√2, far too
steep for μ = 1/3. **cosec α = 3** ✗ gives sin α = 1/3 and tan α = 1/(2√2), which is the
result of confusing sin with tan ✓ **None** ✗ is unnecessary, since cot α = 3 is exactly
the condition derived.
**The rule to carry away.** On any surface, slipping begins where **tan(slope angle) =
μ** ✓ Everything else here is the geometry of saying where that is on a sphere.
∴ cot α = 3.

The string must supply the centripetal force, so the breaking tension sets a ceiling on
ω².
**Step 1 — write the centripetal requirement.** For a ball of mass m on a string of
length L swung in a horizontal circle, the tension provides the inward force:
T = m ω² L
**Step 2 — set T to its greatest safe value.**
324 = (0·5) ω² (0·5)
324 = **0·25 ω²**
**Step 3 — solve.**
ω² = 324/0·25
= **1296**
**ω = 36 rad s⁻¹** ✓
**Why ω² and not ω.** The centripetal acceleration is **ω²r**, so the tension grows with
the **square** of the angular speed ✓ Doubling the spin rate quadruples the pull, which
is why strings break so suddenly as the speed is raised.
**A check on the other quantities.**
v = ωL = 36 x 0·5 = **18 m s⁻¹**
and T = mv²/L = 0·5(324)/0·5 = **324 N** ✓ the same tension by the linear form of the
formula.
**How large that tension is.** 324 N is the weight of about **33 kg** - more than sixty
times the ball's own weight of 4·9 N ✓ which is why the weight of the ball is neglected
here and the circle treated as truly horizontal.
**A note on the geometry.** Strictly, a ball swung on a string about a vertical axis
hangs slightly below the horizontal, and the string's radius is a little less than L. But
with the tension sixty times the weight the string is within about **1°** of horizontal ✓
so taking the radius as L is an excellent approximation and is what the question intends.
**Reading the distractors.** **18** ✗ is the **linear** speed v in m s⁻¹, not the angular
speed - the commonest slip, since both appear in the working. **9** ✗ is half of 18, and
**27** ✗ matches no step ✓ The units in the question ("radian/s") are the hint that 18,
a velocity, cannot be the answer.
∴ 36 rad/s.
